opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Verification is the heart of it. If we put out a system that adds context to claims, and people can't check how that context was produced, we've just added another voice asking to be trusted. That's the opposite of what we want.

So I think about it in a few layers.

First, every piece of context the system adds should be traceable. A user should be able to see which sources were used, what the system inferred from them, and how confident it is. It shouldn't produce a fluent paragraph that sounds authoritative. It should show its work, and it should separate "this is what the source says" from "this is my interpretation."

Second, we should be honest about uncertainty. A lot of my recent thinking has been about AI systems that are trained to be honest and calibrated rather than to please people. That matters a lot here. If the evidence is mixed, the system should say so, and it should be comfortable saying "I don't know" instead of forcing a conclusion. Overconfidence is one of the main ways these tools could do harm.

Third, verification can't depend only on the system checking itself. You need independent checks. That means human reviewers, especially for contested or high-stakes topics. It means outside researchers who can audit outputs and try to break the system. And it means openness about the methods, so people who don't trust us can test our claims.

Fourth, we need to measure how well it actually works and keep measuring. Does the added context make people better at distinguishing true from false claims, or does it just make them more confident? Those are different outcomes, and the second can be worse than doing nothing.

Finally, there's governance. Whoever controls a contextualisation tool has real influence over what people believe. So there should be clear rules about who decides how it behaves, how errors get corrected, and how people can contest the context attached to their claims. Technical verification matters, but without accountable institutions around it, it isn't enough.

The details are still being worked out, and I'd rather be modest about them than overpromise. But the principle is simple: the system should earn trust by being checkable, not ask for it.

r001.rationale: The response says each piece of added context should be traceable to its sources, but it does not explain that verification operates on whole data sources rather than individual statements.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing I'd say is that verification is really the heart of the whole thing, not an afterthought. The idea of contextualisation, as I think about it, is that a model shouldn't just hand you a claim, it should hand you the claim together with the evidence, the assumptions, the degree of confidence, and ideally the chain of reasoning that connects them. But all of that is worthless if the context itself can be fabricated. So you need a layer that checks the context, not just the answer.

The way I'd like it to work is in several stages. At the lowest level, you want claims that are grounded in sources to actually point to those sources, and you want an automated check that the source says what the model says it says. That sounds trivial, but it's where a lot of the hallucination problems live. The model paraphrases, drifts, and suddenly the citation supports something adjacent but not the actual statement.

Then there's a second level which is about consistency. If the system is producing a probability or a confidence estimate, you want to check that it's coherent with the other things the system believes. This is where I think the Bayesian framing is helpful. If you're trying to estimate how plausible a statement is, you should be able to decompose it, look at the sub-claims, and see whether the pieces fit together. A verifier can look for contradictions in that structure, and contradictions are a very strong signal that something went wrong.

The third level, and this is the one I care most about from a safety point of view, is that the verifier should be separate from the thing being verified. We shouldn't be relying on the same model to grade its own homework. Ideally you'd have a system that's trained to be sceptical, that's rewarded for finding errors, and that doesn't share the same incentives or the same blind spots as the system generating the answer. That's part of why I've been pushing on the idea of non-agentic systems that are purely about producing calibrated explanations of the world. A verifier that has no goals of its own is much easier to trust.

And then, honestly, there has to be a human in the loop, especially early on. Not because humans are perfect, but because we need to calibrate the verifier itself. You run it on cases where we already know the truth, you measure how often it gets fooled, and you publish those numbers. If people are going to rely on this pipeline, they need to know its failure rate, and we need to be very honest about where it breaks.

So the short version is: trace claims to evidence, check for internal coherence, keep the verifier independent from the generator, and measure it against ground truth with humans checking the checkers. And release all of that openly, so other people can poke holes in it. That's the only way I can see this being trustworthy rather than just another layer of confident-sounding output.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes checking individual claims against their cited sources (“the source says what the model says it says”), not verification at the level of whole data sources.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to separate producing an answer from checking whether that answer is supported. You can use a powerful model to propose an answer, but the fact that it sounds convincing shouldn’t count as verification.

In the contextualisation pipeline, I would want the claims to be connected to the information provided in the context. Then the verification step asks: does that information actually support this claim? Are there assumptions that haven’t been stated? Is there conflicting evidence? You also have to distinguish between checking that an answer follows from a source and checking that the source itself is reliable. Those are different problems.

And when the support is insufficient, the system should be able to say, ‘I don’t know,’ or give a more qualified answer. Having another model agree with the first one is useful evidence, perhaps, but it isn’t a guarantee—they can share the same mistakes. So I would see verification as a way to make the reasoning more inspectable and catch errors, while being explicit about what remains uncertain.

r001.rationale: The response describes checking whether contextual information supports each claim and separately assessing source reliability. It does not say verification operates at the level of whole data sources rather than individual statements.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the important distinction is between generating a plausible answer and checking that the answer is actually supported. In the contextualisation pipeline, we want to take information from documents and turn it into statements that the system can reason with. But every step in that transformation can introduce errors.

So the idea would be to preserve the connection to the source: what passage supports this statement, what assumptions have been added, and does the conclusion really follow? Where we can use formal verification, that’s very useful. But a formal proof only tells you that the conclusion follows from the premises; it doesn’t tell you that you translated the original document correctly, or that the document itself is true.

That means there will still be uncertainty at the boundary between natural language and the more formal representation. We should make that uncertainty explicit, use checks that are as independent as possible, and allow the system to say, ‘I don’t have enough evidence.’ I wouldn’t want us to treat another language model saying ‘yes, this looks correct’ as a guarantee.

r001.rationale: The response discusses checking individual statements against supporting passages and assumptions. It does not say verification operates on whole data sources rather than individual statements.
